transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-08 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood Solutions) | Daniel Park (Zenith Head Eng), Maya Singh (Quant Lead), Liam O'Connor (CFO), Ivy Zhou (Infra)

Auto-generated Summary (optional): Discussed cost per token, batching and KV cache leverage to reduce unit cost, and options for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment. Agreed to run benchmarks and share cost modeling spreadsheet.

00:00 Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making the time. This is Alex on the AE side, Priya is our SE, Samir's on solutions. Quick agenda: we want to understand your workloads, budget & constraints, and walk through how Redwood can change unit economics via batching, caching, and dedicated capacity.
00:13 Daniel Park: Yup, great, thanks. Quick intro, I'm Daniel, head of eng. Maya runs the quant teams, Liam's on for budget and infra is Ivy. We run a live signals pipeline and an experiment cluster for model training inference. Latency is critical for signals but we also have nightly bulk runs.
00:30 Maya Singh: yes, and to add we're hitting cost pain from per-token pricing with our current provider, and batching is limited cause of tail latency on small N requests. We want to understand tradeoffs — is dedicated worth it?
00:45 Priya Nair: cool, that's exactly the right question. To set expectations: hosted API is fastest to get started and usually the best for spiky low-volume latency-sensitive calls. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools so predictable throughput and lower unit cost if you commit. Private (VPC/on-prem) is for data residency and extra controls — costs vary based on infra.
01:10 Liam O'Connor: Our CFO here — curious about per-token math. We did some roughs: at current provider it's like $0.0009 per token for generation, embeddings more; that burns through budget fast. Can Redwood get below that?
01:25 Alex Chen: short answer: often yes, especially on dedicated. But it's workload-dependent. We typically break down unit economics into model choice, quantization, batching, caching (prefix/KV), and request routing. For example, continuous KV cache for chat history reduces repeated encoder cost and can drop per-response token count substantially.
01:45 Maya Singh: give us an example — we have 80ms p50 latency target for live signals and 300ms p95 max. Average response length small-ish — 20-60 tokens. But we do 3M calls/day during market hours.
02:05 Priya Nair: ok that's helpful. With short responses, you want to avoid batching that increases tail latency. But you can still gain by model selection + quantization; switching to a 4-bit quantized variant reduces FLOPS and cost per token a lot. Also prefix caching helps if requests share prefixes — e.g., many of your prompts likely share preambles.
02:30 Daniel Park: we do share a lot of boilerplate — same context, different tickers. How much can caching save?
02:40 Priya Nair: depends on reuse. If caching saves you from re-encoding the static prompt, you can cut token compute roughly in half for those calls. In practice, customers see 15-60% per-token compute reduction depending on reuse patterns.
03:02 Samir Patel: and batching: on Dedicated you can configure batching windows and max batch sizes to hit throughput goals while respecting latency SLOs. For example, if you can tolerate ~30ms extra latency you can batch and drop unit cost substantially — but for 80ms p50 target we wouldn't want large batching on live path. We might route low-latency live traffic to dedicated low-burst pools and route batchable loads to cheaper capacity or night windows.
03:30 Ivy Zhou: for VPC/private, what's the overhead? Our security team will ask about KMS and audit logs. Also curious if private deployment impacts per-token cost direct?
03:40 Priya Nair: private adds infra costs (your cloud/GPU ops) plus Redwood platform fee. Unit runtime cost is mostly the GPU cost and utilization. With private, you control instance types and can sometimes get better long-term economics if you have bulk infra discounts. But there's operational overhead. For per-token pricing we provide guidance and recommendations on model/quantization, but the underlying GPU cost remains your bill (for private).
04:10 Liam O'Connor: ok. Back to numbers — can you sketch host vs dedicated per-token numbers for a mid-size LLM?
04:18 Alex Chen: sure, ballpark: hosted for a popular open model might be $0.0012–$0.0020 per generated token (includes Redwood margin & infra). Dedicated reserved capacity can drop effective per-token compute cost to $0.0005–$0.0012 depending on commit level, model choice and utilization. And with caching & quantization you can effectively halve the cost for certain workloads. These are examples — we'll send a spreadsheet with modeled scenarios.
04:45 Maya Singh: that matches our intuition. For 3M calls/day at 40 tokens avg, that's 120M tokens/day. Even a $0.0008 delta is significant monthly.
05:00 Priya Nair: exactly — that's why we focus on levers: batching where acceptable, prefix/KV caching, and choosing quantized model variants. Also model routing: send latency-critical calls to higher-cost low-latency pools, and bulk scoring to cheaper backfill capacity.
05:25 Daniel Park: how do you handle tail latency? We worry about p99s during market open spikes.
05:32 Priya Nair: tail latency is addressed by reserved capacity, autoscale policies, and pre-warming. Dedicated pools with headroom, and smart routing can fallback to other regions or model variants. We also expose trace-level metrics so you can see token-level latencies and tokenization hotspots.
06:00 Maya Singh: any gotchas with batching & stateful chat? Our quant researchers do multi-turn sessions, large KV cache size. Do caches persist across nodes?
06:12 Samir Patel: caches are per-serving instance but we support sticky routing or centralized KV caching for certain deployments; for high reuse we recommend a cache hit strategy to keep the hot prefixes in memory. There are tradeoffs with stateful scaling but we can design for it.
06:30 Ivy Zhou: about security: SOC2 ok? SAML for SSO? Do you support customer-managed KMS?
06:38 Alex Chen: yes SOC2 Type II, we integrate with SAML/SSO, RBAC. For Dedicated and Private we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations for key material, and audit logs. We'll share docs.
06:52 Liam O'Connor: for cost modeling, is there a way to estimate utilization breakeven for dedicated commit? Like how many tokens/day to justify a monthly committed instance?
07:05 Priya Nair: yes — we calculate breakeven based on committed v. on-demand unit price and utilization. For example, a single A100-equivalent node with high utilization serving a quantized model could realize unit cost reduction at around X tokens/day (we'll compute exact using your batch and prompt shapes). We'll model scenarios in the spreadsheet.
07:30 Maya Singh: ok we'll provide a representative prompt set. Also want to run an actual benchmark — ideally on dedicated nodes to see real p95/p99 and cost.
07:42 Alex Chen: we can run a 2-hour benchmark with your prompt set, simulate market-hour concurrency, and return p50/p95/p99 and cost per token breakdown. Priya will lead that.
07:55 Daniel Park: good. A few more items — how do you handle model updates and version pinning? Our compliance needs ability to pin versions and audit outputs for a window.
08:05 Priya Nair: we support model versioning and rollout policies, can pin to specific model+quant combination, and outputs are logged for audit per your retention policy. For Private, logs stay in your VPC.
08:20 Lydia (crosstalk, unclear): [unintelligible]...
08:26 Maya Singh: small question: what about embeddings costs? We're doing embeddings for similarity search and they blow up cost too.
08:32 Alex Chen: embeddings typically charged differently — per vector or per token depending on model. We can advise on model choices and batching embeddings to reduce overhead. For large-scale similarity indexing, many customers run embeddings on dedicated cheaper nodes overnight and bulk update indexes to reduce peak spend.
08:55 Liam O'Connor: ok, this is all helpful. I want to make sure we capture next steps — run benchmark, send spreadsheet, share security docs.
09:05 Alex Chen: yes summary: we'll send cost model spreadsheet, schedule benchmark, and share security + network docs. Any other stakeholder we should loop in?
09:15 Daniel Park: our infra lead Ivy is here; after the benchmark we'll loop in the legal and procurement folks.
09:22 Maya Singh: timeline — we'd like a decision in 4–6 weeks if numbers line up.
09:28 Alex Chen: noted. We'll aim to get the spreadsheet and SOC docs by Tue (Mar 10) and propose benchmark slots for week of Mar 22.

Transcript ends.

Notes on transcription: occasional name misrecognitions, some technical terms abbreviated. The team asked for sample prompts and will provide them via shared drive link (Maya to upload).
